About: radial-velocity curves of a double-lined spectroscopic binary, and the masses M sin3 i they give

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the radial velocity vr of star 1 (text colour) and star 2 (orange) against t/Porb from 0 to 2, traced up to the time cursor, about the dashed line vsys = +30 km/s. Right: the two orbits seen from above the orbital plane (face on), ±0.22 AU about the centre of mass (cross), with the dashed line of nodes (ascending node of star 1 on the right), the periastron of star 1 ticked, a 0.1 AU scale bar, stars drawn to scale, and on each star an arrow of vr − vsys, up and red when receding, down and blue when approaching.
Controls
Masses M1 and M2 (1.0 to 4.0 M⊙), eccentricity e (0 to 0.6), argument of periastron ω (0° to 360°) and inclination i (30° to 90°). Changing any of them clears the curves and restarts both stars from periastron.
Measured
vr from the exact Kepler orbit for Porb = 10 days split between the stars by the centre-of-mass frame; K1 and K2 are the semi-amplitudes; M1 sin3 i and M2 sin3 i are found from K1, K2, e and Porb as an astronomer would. One period is 8 s on screen. The Readouts panel groups the time, the line-of-sight velocities, the semi-amplitudes and the masses from the curves.
What the spectrum cannot tell
A spectrum measures only the velocity along the line of sight, v sin i for the orbit, so the masses found from the curves are M1 sin3 i and M2 sin3 i: lower limits, equal to the true masses only when the orbit is edge on. The inclination must come from elsewhere, such as eclipses. The model is two point masses in an exact Kepler orbit, with no tides or third body.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two stars, one centre of mass

Set M1 = 2.0 M⊙, M2 = 1.0 M⊙, e = 0, ω = 0° and i = 90°. Before watching the curves being traced, predict how the swings in velocity of the two stars compare.

2 · A heavier star 1

Keep M2 = 1.0 M⊙, e = 0, ω = 0° and i = 90°, and before raising M1 from 2.0 M⊙ to 4.0 M⊙ predict what happens to the semi-amplitude K1 of star 1. Then raise it and watch the readouts.

3 · An eccentric orbit

Set M1 = 2.0 M⊙, M2 = 1.0 M⊙, ω = 0° and i = 90°, and before raising e from 0 to 0.5 predict the shape of the curve of star 1. Then raise it and watch the curve being traced.

4 · Turning the orbit, ω = 90°

Keep M1 = 2.0 M⊙, M2 = 1.0 M⊙, e = 0.5 and i = 90°, and before setting ω = 90° predict how the curve of star 1 changes. Then set it and watch one period being traced.

5 · A tilted orbit

Keep M1 = 2.0 M⊙, M2 = 1.0 M⊙, e = 0.5 and ω = 90°, and before lowering i from 90° to 30° predict what the readouts M1 sin3 i and M2 sin3 i will show. Then lower it and read them.

6 · Summary: weighing a binary from its spectrum

The two stars go round their common centre of mass on opposite sides of it, so K1/K2 = M2/M1: the heavier star swings less. An eccentric orbit gives a lopsided curve whose shape fixes e and ω.

From K1, K2, e and Porb the spectrum gives M1 sin3 i and M2 sin3 i, lower limits on the masses. The true masses need the inclination from elsewhere, for example from eclipses, which happen only when i is close to 90°.

Weighing the Stars of a Binary

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

This sim traces the radial velocities of the two stars of a double-lined spectroscopic binary and shows their orbits from above. Sliders set M1, M2, the eccentricity e, the argument of periastron ω and the inclination i.

What you'll learn

  • How a star's speed along the line of sight, vr, becomes a curve (notes, section 2.2).
  • What the semi-amplitudes K1 and K2 say about the two stars.
  • How e, ω and i shape the curves, and which masses a spectrum can give.
One star on its orbit about the centre of mass. Only the part of its velocity along the line of sight, vr, shifts its spectral lines (equation 2.19).

What's on screen

  • Left: vr of star 1 (text colour) and star 2 (orange) against t/Porb from 0 to 2, traced up to the time cursor, about the dashed line vsys = +30 km/s.
  • Right: the two orbits seen from above the orbital plane, observer below. The cross is the centre of mass, the dashed line the line of nodes, and the tick the periastron of star 1.
  • Arrows on the stars: vr − vsys, up and red when the star recedes, down and blue when it approaches.
See itLook at the opening values. Watch for: the two curves being traced against time, and the arrows on the two stars flipping between red and blue.

03

The lighter star swings more, because it sits further from the centre of mass

Both stars circle the centre of mass with the same period Porb, so each star's speed is 2π times its distance from that point, divided by Porb. Only the part along the line of sight is seen. On a circular orbit it is a cosine whose amplitude is the semi-amplitude K (2.20):

Equation (2.20). a1 and a2 are the orbit radii about the centre of mass.

The centre of mass stays put, so M1 a1 = M2 a2. Dividing the two amplitudes gives (2.21):

Equation (2.21). The star with the larger swing is the less massive.
The opening masses, e = 0, i = 90°. Star 2 is orange, as on the sim.

At M1 = 2.0 and M2 = 1.0 M⊙, star 2 has half the mass, so twice the orbit and twice the swing: K1 = 47.5 km/s and K2 = 95.0 km/s.

Key idea. The pull between the stars is equal on both. It is the position of the centre of mass that sets who swings more.
See itLook at the two curves at the opening masses. Watch for: the orange curve reaching twice as far from the dashed line as the text-coloured one, with K1 reading 47.5 and K2 reading 95.0 km/s.
04

A heavier star 1 lowers its own swing K1

Raising M1 does speed up the relative orbit, because Kepler's third law makes a³ grow with M1 + M2 at a fixed period. But star 1's share of that orbit is M2/(M1 + M2), and the share falls faster. Putting a1 = aM2/(M1 + M2) into (2.20) gives:

Circular orbit, fixed Porb. The relation on the right follows from Kepler's third law.

Keep M2 = 1.0 M⊙ and raise M1 from 2.0 to 4.0 M⊙. The relative speed 2πa sin i/Porb rises from 142.5 to 169.0 km/s, but star 1's share falls from 1/3 to 1/5. So K1 falls from 47.5 to 33.8 km/s, while K2 rises from 95.0 to 135.2 km/s.

Key idea. A heavier star moves less, even when it makes the whole system faster.
See itRaise M1 to 4.0 M⊙ and read the semi-amplitudes. Watch for: the text-coloured curve shrinking while the orange one grows, with K1 reading 33.8 and K2 reading 135.2 km/s.
05

The two swings give the masses, up to a factor sin³ i

Adding the two swings gives K1 + K2 = 2πa sin i/Porb, where a = a1 + a2. Cubing it and using Kepler's third law removes a, and leaves the masses in terms of what the spectrum measures (2.22, 2.23):

Equation (2.23). G is the gravitational constant, and the readouts M1 sin3 i and M2 sin3 i are these.

On an eccentric orbit each K carries a factor 1/√(1 − e²). The notes' mass function brings the matching factor (1 − e²)3/2, and the sim applies it to the sum:

The notes' factor (1 − e²)3/2 is 1 when e = 0.
M1 M2 e i

These sliders move the sim too. The numbers come from the sim's own audit function.

See itSet M1 = M2 = 2.0 M⊙. Watch for: the two curves becoming mirror images, with K1 and K2 both reading 78.4 km/s and each M sin3 i reading 2.00 M⊙.
06

An eccentric orbit bends the curve, and the bend gives e and ω

On an eccentric orbit star 1 rushes through periastron and dawdles near apastron, so its curve is no longer a sinusoid. For eccentricity e and argument of periastron ω (2.26):

Equation (2.26). θ is the true anomaly, measured from periastron.

With ω = 0 periastron lies at the ascending node, where star 1 recedes fastest. At e = 0.5 the curve has a sharp maximum of 112.3 km/s, which is K1(1 + e) = 82.3 km/s above vsys, and a broad, shallow minimum only K1(1 − e) = 27.4 km/s below it. The star spends 66% of the period below vsys.

Star 1 at e = 0.5, M1 = 2.0 M⊙, M2 = 1.0 M⊙, i = 90°, with time measured from periastron, as in the notes' Figure 14.

With ω = 90° the star passes periastron furthest behind the plane of the sky, moving across the line of sight. The curve falls from its maximum to its minimum in about 0.20 Porb, and rises slowly back over the other 0.80, between K1 above and below vsys.

See itRaise e to 0.5 with ω = 0°. Watch for: a tall narrow peak reaching 112.3 km/s and a broad shallow trough, with K1 reading 54.9 km/s.
See itNow turn ω to 90°. Watch for: the curve rising slowly to 84.9 km/s and dropping steeply through the minimum, with the periastron tick of star 1 at the top of the orbit view.
07

A tilted orbit hides the mass: the spectrum gives only M sin³ i

Tilting the orbit multiplies every line-of-sight velocity by sin i and leaves the shape of the curves alone. The masses depend on the cube of those velocities, so the spectrum gives M sin3 i, a lower limit on each mass that equals the mass only when the orbit is edge on, at i = 90° (notes, section 2.2).

isin isin3 iM1 sin3 iM2 sin3 i
90°1.0001.0002.00 M⊙1.00 M⊙
60°0.8660.6501.30 M⊙0.650 M⊙
45°0.7070.3540.707 M⊙0.354 M⊙
30°0.5000.1250.250 M⊙0.125 M⊙

For M1 = 2.0 M⊙ and M2 = 1.0 M⊙. The readouts do not depend on e or ω.

At i = 30° the velocities halve but the readouts fall to an eighth. Their ratio is still 2, because both curves shrink together, so the ratio of the masses survives while their sizes do not. The inclination has to come from elsewhere: eclipses occur only when i is close to 90°, where sin i is close to 1.

See itLower i to 30° at e = 0.5 and ω = 90°. Watch for: both curves shrinking to half their size, with K1 reading 27.4 and K2 reading 54.9 km/s, and the masses reading 0.250 and 0.125 M⊙.
08

Summary

In one line. A spectrum measures each star's speed along the line of sight, and the two curves, with the period, fix what can be known about the masses.
  • K1/K2 = M2/M1: the heavier star swings less.
  • (M1 + M2) sin3 i = (1 − e²)3/2 Porb(K1 + K2)³/2πG, so the masses are known only up to sin³ i.
  • The shape of the curve fixes e and ω.

Common mix-ups

  • "The heavier star swings more, because it pulls harder." The forces are equal: K1 = 47.5 and K2 = 95.0 km/s at 2.0 and 1.0 M⊙.
  • "A heavier star 1 makes K1 larger." Its share of the orbit falls: K1 goes from 47.5 to 33.8 km/s.
  • "An eccentric orbit just gives a taller sinusoid." At ω = 0 the maximum is narrow and the minimum broad.
  • "Tilting to 30° halves the masses." The velocities halve. The masses go as their cube, so they fall to an eighth.

Things to try on your own

  • At i = 90° raise e from 0 to 0.5. K1 and K2 grow by 1/√(1 − e²) = 1.155, yet the masses stay at 2.00 and 1.00 M⊙.
